title: HPC Workload Characterisation Questionnaire
description: This questionnaire collects factual information about your research workloads so that the HPC Users' Committee can design and assign appropriate Quality-of-Service (QoS) classes. You are asked to describe what you observe and what evidence you have — the committee applies the agreed tests and makes the policy judgements.
coreNotice: Users provide facts and evidence. The committee applies the agreed tests. You are not being asked to assess your own priority, entitlement, or queue. Incomplete technical knowledge does not disadvantage your submission — 'Don't know' is always a valid answer.

sections.title: A. Research Programme
sections.description: This section collects basic contextual information about your research group. You are not being asked to classify your research as computational, experimental, or theoretical. All research groups are equally welcome to use the facility.

questions.label: Research group name
questions.placeholder: e.g. Sharma Group / Computational Materials Lab
questions.helpText: The name by which your group is commonly known within the department.

questions.label: Department / School
questions.helpText: Select the department or school your group belongs to.

questions.label: Department / School (if 'Other')
PI salutation
Principal Investigator (PI) — full name
PI email address
questions.helpText: Used for correspondence from the HPC Users' Committee. The PI will be sent a summary to review before the submission is finalised.

questions.label: Is the PI filling out this form?

options.label: No — another group member is completing the technical sections

questions.label: Name of person completing this form
questions.helpText: The person running the calculations often knows the workload in greatest detail.

questions.label: Email address of person completing this form
Role of person completing this form
questions.helpText: Select the role that best describes your position within the group.

questions.label: Role (if 'Other')
Brief description of research activities for which HPC resources are used or requested (optional)
questions.placeholder: Describe the research problems your group is working on that involve or would involve HPC computation. For example: 'First-principles calculations of transition-metal oxide surfaces for catalysis; molecular dynamics of protein-membrane interactions.'
questions.helpText: Please be factual and descriptive. You do not need to argue that the research is important or computationally intensive — just describe what you do.

sections.title: B. Workload Profile
sections.description:
This section collects information about the software and codes your group uses, and the broad character of your workloads. Please add one entry per principal application or code. You may add as many codes as apply.

Throughout this questionnaire, a 'job' means a single submission to the HPC scheduler — one entry in the queue. For example, 100 separate calculations submitted individually are 100 jobs. A job array submitted as a single scheduler entry also counts as one job, even if it runs many independent tasks internally.

questions.label: Principal applications and codes used
questions.helpText: Add one entry per application or code that your group uses or plans to use on the HPC facility. If you are unsure whether to include a code, include it.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups are not natively supported in Google Forms. When exporting to Google Forms, implement as a separate linked Google Form (one submission per code entry) or as a fixed set of rows (e.g. Code 1, Code 2, …). The React prototype stores this as an array of row objects.

subQuestions.label: Application / code name
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. VASP, GROMACS, Gaussian, OpenFOAM, custom code
subQuestions.helpText: The name of the application. For in-house or custom codes, describe briefly (e.g. 'In-house Monte Carlo code (Fortran)').

subQuestions.label: Version (if known)
Software website or publication reference (if known)
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. https://www.vasp.at or DOI

subQuestions.label: Workload type(s) for this code
subQuestions.helpText: Select all categories that describe the type of computation this code performs. These categories describe the workload, not your research identity.

subQuestions.label: Workload type description
subQuestions.placeholder: Please describe the type of computation

subQuestions.label: Approximate number of production jobs per year using this code
subQuestions.helpText: Include all jobs, including short test runs if they are frequent. A rough estimate is sufficient.

subQuestions.label: Notes on this code (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: Any additional information about how this code is used by your group.

sections.title: C. Typical Job Setup
sections.description:
For each code or application you run on HPC, describe how you typically set up a job — which system you run it on and approximately what resources you use.

You do not need to know exact hardware specifications. Range estimates and "Don't know" are always valid answers. If you run the same code on different systems, or in very different configurations, add a separate entry for each.

questions.label: Typical job setups
questions.helpText: Add one entry per (code, system) combination. For example, if you run VASP on the IISER cluster and also on a national facility, add two entries.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups require a separate linked Google Form or fixed-row approach.

subQuestions.label: Which application or code does this job setup apply to?
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. VASP, GROMACS, OpenFOAM, in-house Python script
subQuestions.helpText: Enter the name of the software this entry describes. Use the same name as in Section B. If this setup applies to all your codes generally, leave blank.

subQuestions.label: Name of the cluster, facility, or computer where this job runs
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. IISER Bhopal HPC, PARAM Shakti, collaborator cluster at IIT Delhi, my desktop workstation
subQuestions.helpText: The name you know the system by — whatever you call it. You do not need to know the technical specification. Examples: 'the IISER cluster', 'PARAM at IIT Bombay', 'my office workstation'.

subQuestions.label: What type of system is this?
subQuestions.helpText: Select the category that best describes the system. This helps the committee understand the context even if the specific hardware is not known.

options.label: HPC cluster — national facility (e.g. PARAM, C-DAC)
HPC cluster — collaborator's or another institution's
Cloud computing (e.g. AWS, Google Cloud, Azure)
Workstation or shared server (multi-core, not a cluster)

subQuestions.label: Approximately how many compute nodes does a typical job use?
subQuestions.helpText: A 'node' is one physical computer in the cluster. Most jobs use between 1 and 4 nodes. If you run on a single desktop or laptop, select '1 node'. If you are not sure, select 'Don't know'.

subQuestions.label: Approximately how many CPU cores does a typical job use in total?
subQuestions.helpText: Total cores across all nodes. If you requested 4 nodes and each node has 32 cores, the total is 128 cores. A rough estimate is fine — 'Don't know' is also valid.

subQuestions.label: Does this job use GPUs?
subQuestions.helpText: GPUs are specialised processors used to accelerate certain calculations (e.g. machine learning, molecular dynamics with GPU-enabled codes). If you are not sure, select 'Don't know'.

subQuestions.label: How many GPUs does each node have in this setup?
subQuestions.helpText: The number of GPUs on each compute node used for this job. If you are not sure, select 'Don't know'.

subQuestions.label: GPU model (if known)
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. NVIDIA A100, RTX 3090, V100, Tesla K40
subQuestions.helpText: The name printed on the card or listed in the cluster documentation. Leave blank if you are not sure.

subQuestions.label: Approximately how much memory (RAM) does a typical job use per CPU core?
subQuestions.helpText: Memory per core is more useful than memory per node because node core-counts vary. In Slurm job scripts this is the --mem-per-cpu value. To estimate it: divide the total RAM your job uses by the number of cores it uses. For example, a job using 16 cores and 64 GB RAM needs 4 GB per core.

options.label: More than 32 GB per core (very high memory)

subQuestions.label: Approximately how much scratch disk space does a typical job use?
subQuestions.helpText: The temporary disk space used by the job for input files, output files, and intermediate data while it is running. Think about the size of the files the job produces. 'Don't know' is valid.

options.label: Not applicable — no significant scratch storage used

subQuestions.label: Does this job need fast communication between nodes?
subQuestions.helpText: If your job runs across multiple nodes and the different parts need to communicate frequently during the calculation, it may be sensitive to the speed of the network connecting the nodes. Single-node jobs and jobs where each node runs independently are not sensitive to this. Example of sensitive: a large MPI simulation where all nodes exchange data every timestep. Example of not sensitive: running 100 independent calculations, one per node.

options.label: Yes — the job runs across multiple nodes and communicates frequently between them
No — either single-node, or each node runs independently

subQuestions.label: Any additional notes about this job setup (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 'This is the setup I use on PARAM — I use a smaller setup on the IISER cluster due to queue limits', 'memory use varies a lot depending on system size', 'we have only recently started using GPUs and are still testing configurations'

sections.title: D. Runtime and Wall-Time Behaviour
sections.description:
This section collects observed (resource configuration, wall-clock time) pairs for your workloads.

IMPORTANT: 'Wall time' means the elapsed clock time while a job is actually running — it does NOT include time spent waiting in the queue. Runtime is affected by the resources allocated, so please record the resource configuration alongside each runtime observation.

Please do not enter a single 'required wall time' — instead, enter the wall time that was actually observed for a specific configuration. The committee will analyse these pairs.

If you have already described a typical job setup in Section C, you may cross-reference it here by noting the code and system name.

If your group has not recently used the current IISER HPC cluster, evidence from past usage on other systems, national facilities, or published benchmarks is equally valid. Current cluster usage is not the only accepted source of evidence.

questions.label: Observed runtime records
questions.helpText: Add one entry per (workload, resource configuration) pair for which you have runtime data. If you have run the same calculation on different numbers of cores, add a separate entry for each configuration.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups require a separate linked Google Form or fixed-row approach in Google Forms.

subQuestions.label: Workload / calculation description
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 'VASP geometry optimisation of 64-atom supercell', 'GROMACS 100ns production run'
subQuestions.helpText: A short description of the specific calculation or job type this runtime applies to.

subQuestions.label: Resource configuration for this observation
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 1 node × 32 cores, 128 GB RAM
subQuestions.helpText: Describe the resources that were actually allocated when this runtime was observed. Examples: '1 node × 32 cores, 128 GB RAM' — '4 nodes × 16 cores, 64 GB RAM/node, InfiniBand' — '1 node × 8 cores + 2 × A100 GPUs, 256 GB RAM'. Include nodes, cores, RAM, and GPUs where applicable.

subQuestions.label: Observed wall-clock time (hours)
subQuestions.helpText: How long did the job actually run (excluding queue wait time)? Enter the elapsed wall-clock time.

subQuestions.label: CPU-hours or GPU-hours consumed by this job
subQuestions.helpText: Total core-hours = (number of cores) × (wall-clock hours). For GPU jobs, report GPU-hours = (number of GPUs) × (wall-clock hours). Leave blank if not known.

subQuestions.label: Number of similar jobs in a typical set of jobs
subQuestions.helpText: Approximately how many jobs of this type do you run per year or per research question? Remember: one job = one scheduler submission.

subQuestions.label: Source of this runtime data
subQuestions.helpText: Where does this runtime observation come from? Evidence from any HPC system is valid — current IISER cluster usage is not the only accepted source.

options.label: External or national HPC facility (e.g. PARAM, C-DAC)

subQuestions.label: Evidence confidence level
subQuestions.helpText:
Select the level that best describes the confidence in this runtime observation. These levels indicate evidence quality — they are not used to rank users.

Level 1: Direct production observation — actual jobs with documented resource use and runtime.
Level 2: Reproducible benchmark — a representative calculation on known hardware.
Level 3: Historical/external production evidence — actual production on another HPC system.
Level 4: Software/scaling evidence — published, developer, or vendor information.
Level 5: Projection — estimated future workload without direct measurements.

options.label: Level 1 — Direct production observation (actual production jobs)
Level 2 — Reproducible benchmark (representative calculation on known hardware)
Level 3 — Historical/external production evidence (another HPC system)
Level 4 — Software/scaling evidence (developer or vendor information)

subQuestions.label: Hardware platform (if from an external or historical source)
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. Intel Xeon E5-2680v4, 28 cores/node, EDR InfiniBand
subQuestions.helpText: The compute hardware on which this observation was made. Most relevant for external, national, or historical evidence. Leave blank for current IISER cluster observations.

subQuestions.label: Notes on this runtime observation (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: Any relevant context, e.g. 'job was killed before completion', 'run on a shared workstation, may not be representative of cluster performance'.

questions.label: Would you like the HPC team to run a standard benchmark for any of your codes?
questions.helpText: The HPC facility can run representative benchmark calculations for common codes to provide objective performance data. This is particularly useful if you do not have access to runtime data from the current cluster.

questions.label: Which application(s) would you like benchmarked?

sections.title: N. Your Experience and Workload Characteristics
sections.description: Your answers here determine which follow-up sections the form will show. Only sections relevant to your workload will appear — you will not be asked to complete sections that do not apply. There is no disadvantage to reporting operational difficulties.

questions.label: Which of the following operational problems has your group experienced?
questions.helpText: Select all that apply. If you have not experienced any of these problems, select 'No problems observed'.

options.label: Jobs terminated by the wall-time limit before completion
Excessive waiting time in the queue
Unable to run at the node or core count the workload uses
Jobs failing due to insufficient memory (out-of-memory errors)
Insufficient total capacity — unable to complete all planned calculations
No problems observed — current access has been adequate

questions.label: If 'Other', describe the operational problem
Which of the following workload characteristics apply to your group? Select all that apply.
questions.helpText: These are factual descriptions of how your calculations are organised — not claims about priority or entitlement. Select all that describe your workloads.

options.label: Jobs that run across multiple nodes or cores and may benefit from more parallelism
Use of, or interest in, GPU-accelerated computation
Large numbers of independent jobs (e.g. parameter sweeps, screening calculations)
Sequential pipeline workflows where each step depends on the previous
Extended single calculations that run continuously for long periods

sections.title: E. Wall-Time Termination
sections.description: This section collects factual information about jobs that were stopped by the scheduler because they exceeded the wall-time limit. You are not being asked whether you 'need' a longer wall time — please describe what happened. The committee uses the resource configuration and CPU-hours to assess the nature of the constraint.

questions.label: Has any of your jobs ever been terminated because it exceeded the wall-time limit?
questions.helpText: A job is 'wall-time terminated' when the scheduler kills it because it has been running longer than the time limit set at submission. This is different from a job that crashes or fails for other reasons.

questions.label: Is wall-time termination an isolated occurrence or a recurring pattern?
questions.helpText: Isolated: one or two cases. Recurring: happens regularly to jobs of this type.

questions.label: How many CPU cores were allocated when the job was terminated?
questions.helpText: The number of CPU cores your job was using when it was killed. You can usually find this in your job submission script (e.g. --ntasks or --cpus-per-task × nodes) or in the scheduler's job report. Leave blank if not known.

questions.label: What wall-time limit was requested at submission?
questions.helpText: The wall-time limit that was set when the job was submitted to the scheduler — not how long it actually ran, but the limit it was given.

questions.label: Has the same calculation produced a valid, usable result on any HPC system?
questions.helpText: 'Successfully completed' means the calculation produced a valid, usable result — not just that the job reached the end of its time slot without being killed. If the calculation required multiple checkpoint-restart cycles to finish, that still counts as completion.

options.label: Yes — on the current IISER cluster, in a single uninterrupted run
Yes — on the current IISER cluster, through a series of checkpoint-restart cycles
Yes — on a different HPC system
No — this calculation has not produced a valid result anywhere

questions.label: Which system was this, and what wall-time limit was available?
questions.placeholder: e.g. PARAM Shakti (7-day limit), collaborator cluster at IIT Delhi (5-day limit)
questions.helpText: The name of the system and, if known, the wall-time limit available on that system.

questions.label: How many CPU cores were used in the successful run?
questions.helpText: Leave blank if not known.

questions.label: What wall-time limit was used or available in the successful run?
questions.helpText: The wall-time limit on the system or queue where the calculation completed successfully.

questions.label: Additional notes on wall-time termination (optional)
questions.placeholder: Any other relevant information about wall-time terminations your group has experienced.

sections.title: F. Checkpoint and Restart
sections.description: Checkpoint/restart allows a job to be stopped and later resumed from a saved state, without repeating all completed computation. Add one entry per application or code — different codes may have very different checkpoint/restart capabilities. 'Don't know' is a valid answer for any question.

questions.label: Checkpoint/restart information by code
questions.helpText: Add one entry per application or code. If all your codes behave the same way, one entry is sufficient.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups require a separate linked Google Form or fixed-row approach.

subQuestions.label: Application or code
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. VASP, GROMACS — or leave blank if this applies to all codes

subQuestions.label: Does this application support checkpoint/restart?
subQuestions.helpText: If a job can be stopped and later resumed without repeating completed computation, it supports checkpoint/restart. Examples: GROMACS can write restart files; many codes can resume from a WAVECAR or equivalent.

subQuestions.label: Is checkpoint/restart built into the application, or does it use an external mechanism?
subQuestions.helpText: Native: the application itself writes restart files (e.g. GROMACS .cpt files, VASP WAVECAR). External: a general checkpoint tool (e.g. DMTCP, BLCR) saves the application's memory state.

options.label: Native — the application writes its own restart files
External — a general checkpoint tool is used
Both native and external mechanisms available

subQuestions.label: How frequently are checkpoints written?
subQuestions.helpText: How often does the code save a checkpoint from which it could be restarted?

subQuestions.label: Does the job restart automatically from the checkpoint without manual intervention?
subQuestions.helpText: Manual intervention might include editing input files, copying checkpoint files, or running a separate restart script.

subQuestions.label: Approximately how long does the job take to reinitialise or reload data after a restart?
subQuestions.helpText: Some codes must reload large datasets or reinitialise memory before productive computation resumes. This overhead is in addition to any work lost since the last checkpoint. Enter 0 or leave blank if negligible.

subQuestions.label: Have restarted jobs produced incorrect or unexpected results?
subQuestions.helpText: For example: numerical instabilities, incorrect energies, or results that differ from an uninterrupted run of the same calculation.

subQuestions.label: Has checkpointing been attempted in production and subsequently abandoned?
subQuestions.helpText: Select 'Yes' if your group has tried using checkpoint/restart in practice but stopped using it.

subQuestions.label: Why was checkpointing abandoned?

options.label: Restart overhead too large relative to job runtime
Restarted runs produced incorrect or unreliable results
Not compatible with the job scheduler or cluster configuration

subQuestions.label: If other, please describe
subQuestions.placeholder: Please describe why checkpointing was abandoned

subQuestions.label: Is checkpoint/restart currently used in your production runs?
Additional notes (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: Any additional information about checkpoint/restart for this code.

sections.title: G. Parallel Scaling
sections.description: This section collects factual observations about how your workloads perform when run on different numbers of cores or nodes. Add one entry per code. You are not being asked whether you 'require' a particular number of nodes — please describe what has been observed or is documented.

questions.label: Scaling observations by code
questions.helpText: Add one entry per application or code. For each code you may record multiple resource configurations in the nested scaling data table.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups (and nested repeatable groups) require separate linked Google Forms.

subQuestions.label: Application or code
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. VASP, GROMACS — or leave blank if general

subQuestions.label: Can the workload be divided into independent jobs that do not communicate with each other during execution?
subQuestions.helpText: For example, running 100 independent molecular dynamics trajectories as 100 separate jobs is a highly decomposable workload. In contrast, a single quantum chemistry calculation that uses MPI across 64 cores is tightly coupled.

options.label: Yes — the workload naturally divides into independent jobs
Partly — some steps are independent, others are coupled
No — the workload consists of a single tightly coupled calculation

subQuestions.label: Notes on job independence (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: Describe how the workload is structured if 'partly' or if there is a mixture.

subQuestions.label: Observed runtimes at different resource configurations
subQuestions.helpText: If you have run the same calculation on different numbers of cores or nodes, record the results here. This helps the committee understand how your workload scales.

subQuestions.label: Resource configuration
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. '8 cores (1 node)', '32 cores (1 node)'

subQuestions.label: Observed wall-clock time (hours)
Source of this scaling data
subQuestions.helpText: Evidence from any system is valid — published benchmarks and developer documentation are accepted sources.

options.label: External or national HPC facility (e.g. PARAM, C-DAC)

subQuestions.label: Evidence confidence level
subQuestions.helpText:
Select the level that best describes the confidence in this scaling observation. These levels indicate evidence quality — they are not used to rank users.

Level 1: Direct production observation — actual jobs with documented resource use and runtime.
Level 2: Reproducible benchmark — a representative calculation on known hardware.
Level 3: Historical/external production evidence — actual production on another HPC system.
Level 4: Software/scaling evidence — published, developer, or vendor information.
Level 5: Projection — estimated future workload without direct measurements.

options.label: Level 1 — Direct production observation (actual production jobs)
Level 2 — Reproducible benchmark (representative calculation on known hardware)
Level 3 — Historical/external production evidence (another HPC system)
Level 4 — Software/scaling evidence (developer or vendor information)

subQuestions.label: Published benchmark or documentation reference (if applicable)
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. VASP benchmark suite URL, GROMACS paper DOI, developer website
subQuestions.helpText: Many codes have published scaling benchmarks from developers or literature. If you are using published data, provide the reference here.

subQuestions.label: Notes on this configuration
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 'memory-bound above 32 cores', 'communication overhead significant'

subQuestions.label: Which of the following best describes the observed parallel scaling of this code?
subQuestions.helpText: Select the option that most closely matches what has actually been observed when running this code at different core or node counts. These are factual descriptions of scaling patterns, not quality judgements.

options.label: Approximately linear — wall time roughly halves when cores double
Sub-linear — more cores reduce wall time but with diminishing returns
Plateau observed — performance stops improving beyond a certain core count
Regression observed — performance degrades beyond a certain core count
No parallel scaling — code runs effectively on a single core or thread
Not tested across different core counts

subQuestions.label: Approximately at how many total CPU cores does performance stop improving or begin to degrade?
subQuestions.helpText: Sometimes called the 'strong scaling limit' or 'sweet spot'. Beyond this core count, adding more cores gives little or no benefit for a single job. Leave blank if not known.

subQuestions.label: What is the smallest total number of CPU cores at which this job has been observed to complete?
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 8
subQuestions.helpText: Total cores across all nodes (e.g. 2 nodes × 32 cores = 64 cores). 'Completed' means the calculation produced a valid, usable result — whether in a single uninterrupted run or through a series of checkpoint-restart cycles. Leave blank if not known.

subQuestions.label: What is the largest total number of CPU cores that has been tested?
subQuestions.helpText: Total cores in the largest configuration actually tested — not an ideal or desired maximum. Leave blank if only one configuration has been tried.

subQuestions.label: Additional notes on parallel scaling (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: Any other relevant observations about how your workload scales with resources.

sections.title: H. Memory Requirements
sections.description: This section collects factual information about the memory (RAM) used by your workloads. Add one entry per application or code. Please report observed values where possible.

questions.label: Memory information by code
questions.helpText: Add one entry per application or code. If all your codes have similar memory requirements, one entry is sufficient.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups require a separate linked Google Form.

subQuestions.label: Application or code
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. VASP — or leave blank if general

subQuestions.label: Typical memory used per node
subQuestions.helpText: The RAM typically used by the job on each node during a typical production run.

subQuestions.label: Observed peak memory per node
subQuestions.helpText: The maximum RAM observed at any point during a run. This may be higher than the typical usage. Leave blank if unknown.

subQuestions.label: Minimum memory at which the workload has been observed to run
subQuestions.helpText: The smallest amount of RAM on which the calculation has actually completed. If the calculation has only ever been run on one memory configuration, enter that value.

subQuestions.label: Is the memory usage confined to a single node, or distributed across multiple nodes?
subQuestions.helpText: Per-node: the entire job's memory fits within one node (e.g. a serial or shared-memory parallel job). Distributed: the job uses MPI or similar to spread its memory across many nodes (common in large-scale simulations).

options.label: Per-node — the job fits entirely within a single node's memory
Distributed — the job requires multiple nodes and cannot fit in one node's memory
Either — the job can run on one node but may benefit from distributed memory

subQuestions.label: Has the workload been run on nodes with the standard memory configuration of the current IISER HPC cluster?
subQuestions.helpText: The standard nodes on the current cluster have [standard memory size — to be inserted]. Has the workload been run (or attempted) on nodes with this memory size?

options.label: Yes, but the job failed due to insufficient memory (OOM)
No, not tested on standard nodes

subQuestions.label: Source of this memory information
subQuestions.helpText: Where does this memory information come from? Observed job output, OOM failures, developer documentation, and published benchmarks are all valid sources.

options.label: External or national HPC facility (e.g. PARAM, C-DAC)

subQuestions.label: Evidence confidence level
subQuestions.helpText:
Select the level that best describes the confidence in this memory information. These levels indicate evidence quality — they are not used to rank users.

Level 1: Direct production observation — actual jobs with documented resource use and runtime.
Level 2: Reproducible benchmark — a representative calculation on known hardware.
Level 3: Historical/external production evidence — actual production on another HPC system.
Level 4: Software/scaling evidence — published, developer, or vendor information.
Level 5: Projection — estimated future workload without direct measurements.

options.label: Level 1 — Direct production observation (actual production jobs)
Level 2 — Reproducible benchmark (representative calculation on known hardware)
Level 3 — Historical/external production evidence (another HPC system)
Level 4 — Software/scaling evidence (developer or vendor information)

subQuestions.label: Additional notes on memory requirements (optional)
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 'Memory usage grows with system size — a 200-atom system uses ~50 GB, a 500-atom system uses ~250 GB'.

sections.title: I. GPU and Specialised Resources
sections.description: This section collects factual information about GPU use and performance. Add one entry per application or code that uses, or has been investigated for, GPU acceleration. If none of your workloads use GPUs, this section can be left empty.

questions.label: GPU information by code
questions.helpText: Add one entry per application or code that uses or could use GPU acceleration.
questions.googleFormsNote: GOOGLE FORMS LIMITATION: Repeatable groups require a separate linked Google Form.

subQuestions.label: Application or code
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. GROMACS, PyTorch, VASP, custom ML training script

subQuestions.label: GPU Requirements
What is the GPU use status for this code?
subQuestions.helpText: Select the option that best describes how GPUs are or would be used with this code.

options.label: GPU is currently used in production runs
GPU use is being investigated but not yet in production
This code only runs on GPU — no CPU-only alternative

subQuestions.label: GPU model(s) used, tested, or targeted
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. NVIDIA A100 80 GB, V100 32 GB, RTX 4090
subQuestions.helpText: The GPU hardware used or needed. Leave blank if not known — 'don't know' is fine at this stage.

subQuestions.label: Minimum GPU memory needed per card
subQuestions.helpText: GPU memory determines which GPU models can run this workload. Large ML models (e.g. transformers, diffusion models) often require 40–80 GB. MD and electronic structure codes typically need 16–40 GB.

options.label: Less than 16 GB (standard consumer or entry-level GPU)
16 – 40 GB (e.g. NVIDIA V100 32 GB, A100 40 GB)
More than 80 GB (e.g. H100 NVL — large model or multi-GPU memory pooling)

subQuestions.label: Minimum number of GPUs required per job
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 1
subQuestions.helpText: The smallest number of GPUs on which this job has been observed to complete or is expected to complete.

subQuestions.label: Typical number of GPUs used per job
subQuestions.placeholder: e.g. 4
subQuestions.helpText: The number of GPUs used in a typical production run.

subQuestions.label: GPU-enabled frameworks or libraries used
GPU framework (if 'Other')
subQuestions.placeholder: Please specify

subQuestions.label: Does this workload need fast GPU-to-GPU communication within a single node?
subQuestions.helpText: NVLink is a high-speed connection between GPUs on the same node, used when the workload distributes computation or memory across multiple GPUs simultaneously (e.g. model parallelism in large ML training, or multi-GPU MD). Most single-GPU workloads do not need this.

options.label: Yes — multiple GPUs on the same node must share data at high speed
No — each GPU runs independently or only one GPU is used

subQuestions.label: Does this workload need to use GPUs across multiple nodes?
subQuestions.helpText: Multi-node GPU jobs require high-speed networking (InfiniBand or equivalent) between nodes for GPU communication (e.g. via NCCL for distributed ML training). This is a significant infrastructure requirement. Most GPU workloads at this scale run on a single node.

options.label: Yes — currently done (on collaborator or national facility)
Yes — planned or expected to be needed

subQuestions.label: Approximate number of GPU jobs per year

sections.title: J. Workflow Patterns
sections.description: This section collects information about how your calculations are organised and submitted to the scheduler. HPC facilities serve many research groups simultaneously through time-sharing — jobs from different groups run concurrently and are each served as resources become available. This is different from laboratory instruments, which may need to be reserved exclusively for the duration of an experiment. Understanding the structure of your workflow helps the committee design scheduling policies that allow all groups to make steady research progress.

questions.label: Which of the following patterns describe how your calculations are organised? Select all that apply.
questions.helpText: Select every pattern that applies — your group may use more than one.

options.label: Independent jobs — each job runs separately without depending on the output of other jobs
Sequential pipeline — each step requires the output of the previous step before it can run
Extended single calculations — one calculation that runs continuously as a single job for an extended period

questions.label: Independent Jobs
How many independent jobs do you run per year?
questions.helpText: A rough estimate is sufficient. One job = one scheduler submission. A job array submitted as a single entry counts as one job.

questions.label: Typical wall time per job
questions.helpText: How long does a single independent job typically run?

questions.label: How many independent jobs typically run at the same time?
questions.helpText: The number running concurrently, not the total submitted.

questions.label: Typical time between submitting a job and it completing (including queue wait)?
Total CPU-hours or GPU-hours from independent jobs actually used per year
questions.helpText: The CPU-hours your group actually consumed — as recorded by the scheduler. This may be less than your actual need if access was limited by allocation or queue policies.

questions.label: Total CPU-hours or GPU-hours estimated to be needed per year, if resources were unconstrained
questions.helpText: Your best estimate of annual CPU-hour requirement. Where possible, derive this from Section D: multiply the CPU-hours per job by the number of similar jobs per year. The committee will cross-check this against your Section D data.

questions.label: Sequential Pipeline
How many steps or stages does a typical pipeline have?
questions.helpText: A stage is a step that must wait for the previous step to finish before it can start.

questions.label: Typical wall time per stage
Can any stage of the pipeline be divided into independent parallel jobs?
questions.helpText: For example, if step 3 involves 50 independent calculations that can all run at once, that stage is parallelisable.

questions.label: How many complete pipelines do you run per year?
Typical total time from starting the first stage to completing the last stage
questions.helpText: The total calendar time for one complete pipeline run, including queue waiting between stages.

questions.label: Total CPU-hours or GPU-hours from pipeline jobs actually used per year
questions.helpText: The CPU-hours actually consumed by pipeline jobs as recorded by the scheduler.

questions.label: Total CPU-hours or GPU-hours from pipeline jobs estimated to be needed per year, if resources were unconstrained
questions.helpText: Your best estimate of annual CPU-hour requirement for pipeline workloads. Where possible, derive this from Section D data. The committee will cross-check this against your observed runtime records.

questions.helpText: 'Valid result' means the calculation completed and produced usable output — not just that the job reached the end of its time slot.

questions.helpText: If yes, the calculation may be completable through a series of shorter jobs even if no single job can run for the full required duration. See also Section F.
